client: I started a new job in marketing about six weeks ago, and honestly, I feel like I'm drowning most days. Everyone around me seems so confident and experienced, and I just sit there wondering how long it'll be before they realize I don't belong there. I'm not even sure talking about it will change anything, because the deadlines and the pressure are just... real, they're not going to go away.
therapist: It makes complete sense that you're feeling overwhelmed — starting a new role with real pressure and surrounded by people who seem so polished is genuinely hard, and I'm glad you're giving voice to it even if you're not sure it'll help. I want to gently notice something you said: that feeling of waiting to be "found out" is something so many people experience, and it often tells us more about our inner critic than about our actual competence. What would you say is one specific moment from the past six weeks where you *did* handle something, even imperfectly — something that, if a friend described it, you might actually give them credit for?

client: I guess... there was this one presentation I had to pull together last minute because a colleague got sick, and I did manage to get it done and nobody complained about it. But when I think about it, I mostly just feel relieved it didn't blow up, not actually proud of it. It's hard to see that as a real win when I know I was panicking the whole time and probably just got lucky.
therapist: That's actually a really significant thing you did — stepping up under pressure with little preparation and delivering something that landed well — and I'd love to gently challenge the idea that panicking through it somehow makes it less real. In CBT we'd call what you're doing "discounting the positive," where your mind finds a way to explain away evidence that doesn't fit the story that you don't belong there. What do you think it would take for an achievement to feel "real" to you — and is it possible that standard is one you'd never actually let yourself meet?

client: That question kind of stops me, because honestly I'm not sure what the standard even is. Like, I think I'd need to feel calm and totally in control for something to count as a real achievement, and... I'm starting to see that maybe that never actually happens for anyone. But even if I intellectually get what you're saying about discounting the positive, I don't know how to make myself actually feel it differently, it's not like I can just flip a switch.
therapist: You've just made a really meaningful insight — recognizing that "calm and in control" might be an impossible bar that even the most experienced people around you never actually clear. You're right that understanding something intellectually and *feeling* it differently are two separate things, and that gap is completely normal; the feelings tend to shift gradually through small repeated experiences, not a single switch. I'm wondering — what might it look like to run a tiny experiment this week, where you intentionally notice one moment you handled something and just pause with it for a few seconds, before your mind rushes to explain it away?

client: I hear what you're saying, and the idea sounds simple enough, but I'm honestly worried that in the moment I'll just be too caught up in whatever's happening at work to even remember to do it. And even if I do remember, I feel like my brain will immediately jump to "yeah but that wasn't really a big deal" before I can stop it. I'm not saying I won't try, I just... I don't want to set myself up for another thing to feel bad about if I can't pull it off.
therapist: That kind of self-awareness — anticipating exactly how your mind might sabotage the experiment before it even starts — is actually a really useful thing to bring into the open rather than discover the hard way. So let's make this even smaller and lower-stakes: rather than catching it *in* the moment at work, what if you just spent two minutes at the end of one day this week writing down a single thing that happened, without yet judging whether it "counts"? I'm curious — does removing the pressure to feel anything about it in real time make it feel any more manageable?

client: That does feel a bit more doable, like I can probably manage writing one sentence at the end of the day without it turning into a whole thing. But I'm still a little skeptical, because I feel like I've tried journaling type stuff before and it just ends up feeling mechanical, like I'm going through the motions without it actually meaning anything. I guess I'm willing to try it for one day at least, just... I don't want to promise more than that right now.
therapist: One day is genuinely enough — and I want to say that your caution about over-promising is actually a form of self-knowledge worth respecting, not a sign of resistance. The "going through the motions" feeling you've had with journaling before is worth paying attention to, and it might be a clue that the *why* behind the writing matters as much as the act itself — this isn't about building a habit, it's just one small moment of not letting your mind immediately erase something. What if the only goal for that one sentence is curiosity rather than proof — just noticing what happened, the way you might describe it to a neutral observer, with no pressure for it to mean anything yet?

client: Framing it as curiosity rather than proof does actually feel different somehow, less like I'm trying to convince myself of something I don't believe. I think the pressure I put on journaling before was that it had to fix something or mean something, and maybe that's why it always felt hollow. I'll try it once this week, just one sentence, no judgment... though I'll be honest, part of me is already wondering if I'll just stare at the page and not know what to write.
therapist: That shift you just named — from proof to curiosity — is genuinely meaningful, and the fact that it feels different to you suggests you're not just intellectually agreeing but actually sensing something. For the "staring at the page" worry, it might help to have a simple prompt ready in advance, something like: "One thing that happened today was..." and then just finish the sentence with whatever comes, even if it feels trivial or small. What feels like the most likely moment in your day to do this — is there a natural pause, like after dinner or before bed, where two minutes might actually be available to you?

client: Before bed is probably the most realistic, because I'm usually just scrolling my phone anyway and two minutes feels manageable compared to that. Though I'll be honest, before bed is also when my anxiety tends to spike about the next day, so I'm a little worried it might just open up a whole spiral instead of being a calm two minutes. Maybe I could try it a bit earlier, like right after dinner, and see if that feels less loaded.
therapist: You just did something really healthy there — you noticed a potential obstacle and problem-solved around it yourself, adjusting the plan to fit *your* actual experience rather than forcing yourself into something that might not work. Right after dinner sounds like a genuinely thoughtful choice, and the fact that you're thinking this carefully about it suggests you're more invested in this than your skepticism might let you believe. So just to hold it lightly — one sentence, after dinner, sometime this week, with curiosity rather than pressure: does that feel like something you can carry with you?

client: Yeah, I think I can carry that, it feels small enough that I'm not immediately looking for an exit. I'm a little surprised actually, because I came in here pretty convinced that talking wouldn't change the actual situation at work, and it hasn't, but I feel slightly less like I'm just white-knuckling through it alone. I guess that's something, even if I'm still not sure where any of this leads.
therapist: That closing thought you just shared — "I guess that's something" — is actually you doing the exact same thing we've been talking about, noticing a real shift without immediately explaining it away, and I want to gently point that out. You're right that the deadlines and pressure at work haven't changed, but something in how you're relating to yourself in the middle of it seems to have shifted even slightly, and that's not nothing. As you head into the week, I'm curious — what would it mean for you if "slightly less alone in it" turned out to be a more important thing than you expected?

client: Honestly, that question makes me a little uncomfortable, because if feeling less alone actually matters a lot, that means I've been more isolated in this than I've wanted to admit. I think I've been telling myself the anxiety at work is purely about performance and deadlines, but maybe some of it is just... not having anyone to process it with, and that feels kind of vulnerable to sit with. I'm not sure what to do with that yet, but I don't think I can just dismiss it either.
therapist: The discomfort you're feeling right now is actually a sign that you've touched something real and important, and it takes genuine courage to stay with that rather than immediately moving past it. What you're describing — reframing the anxiety from purely a performance problem to also one of isolation and connection — isn't a weakness, it's a more complete and honest picture of what's actually going on for you. I don't think you need to *do* anything with it just yet; sometimes the most important step is simply letting something be true without rushing to fix it — but I'm wondering, is there anyone in your life, even one person, with whom a small amount of this might feel safe enough to share?

client: There's one friend from my old job who I've stayed in touch with, and I think she'd probably get it, but I haven't really told her how bad some days have been because I don't want to seem like I'm struggling or like I made a mistake taking this new role. I guess I've been performing "fine" with her the same way I feel like I'm performing at work, which is exhausting when I actually think about it. I'm not sure I'm ready to drop that with her yet, but it's strange to realize I've been keeping her at a distance without even meaning to.
therapist: What you just described — performing "fine" in your friendship the same way you do at work — is a really striking connection to make, and the exhaustion you're feeling might partly be because there's almost nowhere right now where you get to just be where you actually are. It makes complete sense that you're not ready to drop that with her yet, and there's no pressure to have a big vulnerable conversation; but I'm curious whether there's a version that feels less like "admitting struggle" and more like just letting one small true thing through — even something as simple as "honestly, some days have been harder than I expected." What do you think she would actually do with that, if you gave her the chance?
